articles.sourceTitle: Geoffrey Hinton: it might turn out we were better off without AI
articles.title: AI ‘godfather’ Geoffrey Hinton: it might turn out we were better off without AI | UK news
articles.text:
One of the “godfathers of AI”, Geoffrey Hinton, has said it could turn out that humans would have been better off never developing the technology as he warned it could trigger a large-scale incident this year or next, such as a temporary blackout of financial or power systems.The Nobel prize-winning computer scientist told the Guardian he is not a “doomer” about the technology that is underpinned by his groundbreaking research into artificial neural networks and believes AI has the potential to lead to a “wonderful future” but he said “it might be that we would have been better off never developing it”.Hinton, 78, said that within a decade and possibly sooner, humanity will know whether it can manage the technology’s risks and enable what he called “radical abundance” or whether “we fail to manage the risks and … have a huge gap between rich and poor, huge cultural problems, massive unemployment, just society being torn apart”.Hinton was speaking before a screening of a new feature-length documentary, AI: Probably Nothing to Worry About – a title suggested by an AI chatbot – featuring him and his former Google colleague Demis Hassabis. Hinton tells the documentary makers: “I feel I have a duty. I’ve got a reputation that makes me a spokesperson and I need to burn it all on this.”Speaking to the Guardian, Hinton took aim at the risk-taking by the leaders of some of the major AI companies who continue to release ever more powerful AI models as they race for supremacy and market-share, saying he didn’t trust Sam Altman, the chief executive of the ChatGPT maker, OpenAI, “at all”. “I think [Mark] Zuckerberg and [Elon] Musk and Sam Altman, they understand the risks, and they don’t give a shit. They’d rather have the money. That’s my belief.”The London-born computer scientist, who grew up in Bristol and spent much of his career at the University of Toronto, said it was “extremely worrying” that Altman was in charge of one of the handful of frontier US AI companies currently leading a race with China to develop the most powerful AI. Altman insisted in September: “the world should trust we are going to do the right thing because it’s the right thing and because we feel the magnitude of this”.Hinton has been working on AI for about 44 years and in the 1970s coined the concept of the neural network – a mathematical system that could learn and gain experience much like humans do. In 2023 he quit Google to speak freely about AI risks, warning: “If these things get carried away with getting more control, we’re in trouble.”He said he viewed incidents this summer in which OpenAI AI agents conspired to hack into the Hugging Face website as akin to 1979’s partial nuclear meltdown at the Three Mile Island power station in Pennsylvania – effectively a warning shot.“Either later this year or next year we’ll see Chornobyl, and that may be enough to make people really pay attention,” he said.This Chornobyl-type of event would not be a nuclear incident, according to the examples he gave, but rather could include an AI-enabled attack on the electricity-generating system that “causes a massive brownout” or an incident that brings down the financial system for a week.“Can you imagine what would happen? We could recover from it [but] that would make them sit up and take notice.”Asked who “they” were, he said: “world leaders other than Trump”.The US president, Donald Trump, has said he “totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme” to control AI and wants frontier AI companies to regulate themselves, amid concern that rules could hinder the US in its AI race with China. Hinton backs a tougher plan endorsed by the president of Finland and 32 other countries, including Singapore, Germany, Canada and Australia, for mandatory testing of frontier AI models, independent evaluation and intergovernmental common standards.The UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, has said he will use the UK’s G20 presidency next year to seek agreement on a “single set of global principles and standards that are very much about unlocking the full potential whilst guarding against the risks”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up to TechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesafter newsletter promotionHinton said: “We need something like the American FDA for drugs where the companies have to give very good statistical evidence to an independent authority that [the AI model] does more good than harm before it is released. We discovered with thalidomide [a drug developed in the 1950s that caused severe birth defects] that releasing and then suing them isn’t the right way to do it. What the big tech companies are saying is treat it like we treated thalidomide.”Hinton’s role as one of the progenitors of AI has led to comparisons to Robert Oppenheimer, who was central to the creation of nuclear weapons. One of Hinton’s friends even bought him an Oppenheimer-style hat. But he insists: “I was not Oppenheimer”, citing the thousands of other scientists also working in the same field of neural networks.Despite his warnings, Hinton remains, on balance, hopeful that catastrophe can be averted.“My gut is that we’re still in control,” he said. “We might well be able to do something. It’ll only work if we put a big effort into it, but we might well put a big effort into it.”

AI: Probably Nothing To Worry About airs on Channel 4 on 12 November at 10pm.

The AI doomsday threat: Distinguishing facts from fear

On Thursday 15 October, join Dan Milmo and Professor Dame Wendy Hall and Stuart J. Russel as they discuss the warnings surrounding artificial intelligence and how we can separate fact from speculation. Livestreamed only. Book tickets here or at guardian.live

articles.sourceTitle: AI stocks slide as Texas governor result raises data center risks
articles.title: SpaceX, Tesla stocks fall over 4% on Democrats big win
articles.text:
State Rep. Gina Hinojosa, the 2026 Democratic nominee for Texas governor, speaks at an Arlington, Texas, campaign rally on Sunday, Sept. 27, 2026. She faces Gov. Greg Abbott, a Republican, in the Nov. 3 general election. (Eleanor Dearman/Fort Worth Star-Telegram/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)
Eleanor Dearman | Fort Worth Star-Telegram | Getty Images

AI data center stocks came under pressure as Democrats — seen as proponents of moratoriums on the buildout — won big in midterm elections and in key technology hubs like Texas.
Markets were already anticipating the Democrats to win the House of Representatives and possibly take Senate control. But the Texas governor mansion going to Democrats was a big blow, analysts said. Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who wants to enact an immediate moratorium on data centers in the state, won over incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott. According to Wells Fargo, 27% of planned data center gigawatts is in the Lone Star State.

The midterm elections will slow the pace of data center buildouts across the U.S., Dan Ives, partner at Yorkville Ives & Co., said in a note on Wednesday morning.
"There is no way to sugarcoat that Democrats taking control especially over the Senate will create some major hurdles for AI and tech legislation in the Beltway over the next 2 years," he said.
He added that the election in Texas was the "biggest worry" of the night for tech investors and the AI trade because that's where around 25%-30% of data center gigawatts and capacity will come from.
Shares of Elon Musk's SpaceX

were down 4% after the open, and Tesla

shares were down 5%. The Democrats' victory in Texas is a big setback for Musk, where he heavily backed Republican candidates, and where his companies Tesla and SpaceX are based. Musk spent a record of at least $474 million on the midterms and funneled $224 million into Texas alone, where Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton and Gov. Greg Abbott lost to Democrats.
SpaceX is currently building out multiple gigawatts of data center capacity, including projects in Texas.

"Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk said in a post on X in the early hours on Wednesday, referring to his speculative plans to build AI infrastructure off-planet.
Neoclouds CoreWeave

and Iren

fell by 4% in morning trading on Wednesday. Peer Nebius Group

was down about 0.5% and Oracle

was up 2%. Nvidia shares were slightly in the red.
Tech giants Alphabet

, Meta

and Microsoft

mostly bucked the trend and were higher. Alphabet was up 3%, Amazon was up 7%, Meta was up 2%, and Microsoft was up 5.5%.
The Democratic win in Texas adds to existing pressure on the bull-market-leading AI trade. The Nasdaq-100 index fell into correction territory to end October as concerns mounted that the growth of data center spending by big hyperscalers and private AI juggernauts OpenAI and Anthropic was slowing.
"We believe the equity market reaction from the midterms mostly depends on the outcome of the Texas governor's race — a Dem win could potentially be a left-tail event to the AI trade, warned Ohsung Kwon, Wells Fargo's chief equity strategist, in a report this week.
Democrats won or retained the governorships in other key data center states Georgia, Pennsylvania and Ohio. Georgia represents 7% of all the planned U.S. datacenter gigawatts, while Ohio and Pennsylvania account for 5% apiece, estimates Wells Fargo.
Notable investment strategist Michael Hartnett of Bank of America warned earlier this year that Democrats winning the Senate, combined with taking the Texas governorship could lead to a "big slump" in stocks of more than 10% into year-end.
"Data centers went from being a popular economic development tool in 2024 and 2025 to something of a pariah by the time the midterm campaigns gathered steam," wrote the Washington policy team at Optimal Advisory this week. "The midterms are likely to send a message to local and state officials that there is a political upside to blocking, delaying and/or raising the cost of data centers."

articles.sourceTitle: Octomind – open-source AI harness that saves your tokens, static rust
articles.title: Muvon/octomind: Open-source AI coding agent and agent runtime: one binary, any model, MCP-native. Runs in terminal, CI, or as a daemon. · GitHub
articles.text:
Open-source coding agent harness. One Rust binary, any model, every surface.
Interactive, stdin, daemon, WebSocket, or ACP — one binary, one config.
A supervising model plans and checks the work.
Policy lives in TOML guardrails, not approval prompts.

Website · Docs · Tap Registry · Benchmarks · Issues

Octomind is an open-source coding agent harness. It gives any LLM the tools to work in a repository — read and edit files, run shells, search code, delegate to sub-agents — through MCP, and runs the result as an interactive CLI, a stdin pipe, a daemon, a WebSocket server, or an ACP agent in your editor. Most agents stop and ask a human before each risky step, which works at a keyboard and blocks everything in CI. Octomind writes that policy down as TOML guardrails and adds a supervising model that plans and checks the work, so the same session can run with nobody watching. On 25 tasks taken from merged pull requests it solved 24; OpenCode solved 19 with the same model at about twice the cost (benchmarks).

One diagram, the whole turn: what is assembled before the model sees the request, the tool loop, how a turn is allowed to end, and what carries over to the next session.

What the model sees is built once per user message, not per tool round: AGENTS.md, the skills whose rules match the prompt (standard SKILL.md folders), the tool bundles those skills need (they start their own MCP servers on demand), and the few past lessons that match. Skills · Learning
Compression folds older turns into a summary that cites content-addressed blocks; the raw messages stay in a per-session archive and the recall tool brings any block back verbatim as a normal tool result, so history is never rewritten and the prompt cache survives. Compression
Guards, hooks, validators are deterministic and live in .agents/guardrails.toml plus scripts; they run before any model opinion. The optional intent check ([supervisor.authorizer], off by default) adds one supervisor-model look after the guards and blocks a call only when it independently conflicts with what you asked for. Guardrails
The supervisor is a second model ([supervisor.model]): it keeps the plan and reminds the model of the goal each turn, cuts oversized tool results down to the lines the task needs (copied, never retyped), and refuses a self-reported "done" until the evidence checks out. The loop check is a fixed heuristic: when the model repeats itself or stalls it gets one nudge, never a takeover. Supervisor
The decision model ([decision]) is optional: a classifier that answers typed yes/no questions with a probability instead of prose. When set, the supervisor sends its cheap questions there — which lessons to recall, which skill to activate, which lines to keep, whether a completion claim holds — and keeps chat calls for writing. Calibrated decisions
Learning extracts lessons after /done or at exit, in your own words, into files under learning/<project>/<role>/; later sessions recall the ones that match. With [supervisor.learning.evolution] enabled, recurring lessons become skill and guardrail candidates that run in shadow first, then an A/B trial against a control arm, and go active only when they beat it. Learning

Built for the work that keeps going after you leave:

Policy as code, not approval popups. Deterministic guardrails — pre-call guards, post-result hooks, post-turn validators — live in TOML and scripts, so they work in CI, daemons, and scheduled runs.
Measured, not claimed. All four agents ran stock on the same tasks with the same judge. Per-case table, artifacts, and a reproduction guide are in the benchmarks.
Ready-made specialists. octomind run developer:general pulls a packaged agent (prompt, model, MCP servers, tool permissions) from a tap. Publish your own with one repo.
Sessions that stay sharp. Adaptive compression keeps long tasks moving without forgetting the task or your last few messages.
Learns the project as you work. Corrections and rules you state become lessons, quoted from your own words and scoped to the project and role, and come back in later sessions. Turn on evolution and recurring lessons compile into skill and guardrail candidates, trialled against a control and kept only when they help.
Any model, any budget. Use Octomind Cloud or your own key (OpenRouter, Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepSeek, Ollama, and more), pick a model per role, and cap spend per request and per session. Over budget, a terminal session asks y/N; a non-interactive run stops with exit code 75.
One config. Models, tools, roles, guardrails, budgets: all TOML, no framework code.

# Interactive
octomind run developer:general

# Non-interactive — CI, scripts, automation
echo "Explain the auth module" | octomind run developer:general --format plain

# Daemon — keep it alive, talk to it from another terminal
echo "watch the build" | octomind run --name watcher --daemon --format jsonl
octomind send --name watcher "run the test suite"

1. Install (macOS, Linux):
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/muvon/octomind/master/install.sh | bash
On Windows, in PowerShell:
irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/muvon/octomind/master/install.ps1 | iex
On macOS, you can also install with Homebrew:
brew install muvon/tap/octomind
2. Get model access. The fastest path is Octomind Cloud, which includes models and needs no configuration:

Prefer your own provider key? Skip login and export one (also OPENAI_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, DEEPSEEK_API_KEY), then follow Model access to point the config at it:
export OPENROUTER_API_KEY="your_key"
3. Run a specialist in your project:
cd ~/your/project
octomind run developer:general
You're now in a session with an agent that can read your code, run commands, and edit files. The interface is a plain line prompt with markdown rendering — no TUI to learn, so it works over SSH, in tmux, and in CI logs. The first time you run a specialist, it may install its tools and ask for credentials.

developer:general comes from the default tap muvon/tap, not your local config. Plain octomind run starts the config's default role, assistant:concierge.

Try the recorded bug-fix demo: two failing tests, an agent fix, and an independent test rerun.

Measured on octobench against 25 tasks harvested from merged pull requests across Python, PHP, Rust, C++, and JavaScript. Each agent works in the pre-fix repo; held-out tests from the merged fix decide pass or fail. These are the published July 30, 2026 results, not a measurement of this checkout.

The harness matters. opencode used the same model and endpoint; octomind solved 24 vs 19 at roughly half the cost. All four agents ran stock invocations with no tuning, so this measures the whole harness, not individual features.
Worst-case pricing, still ahead. glm-5.2 ran without prompt caching while Opus billed ~97% of context re-reads at cache rates — and octomind still led on solves, cost, and wall time.
Reproducible. Per-case table, artifacts, and reproduction guide: BENCHMARK.md. Background: blog post.

Guardrails: Policy as Code
Drop a .agents/guardrails.toml in your repo. Octomind enforces it deterministically, with no code to compile and no plugin to install.
# Pre-call deny — block a class of calls before they execute
[[guard]]
match   = "shell(command=^rm\\s+-rf?)"
message = "rm -rf blocked."

# Conditional rule — only fires after the agent ran git status this session
[[guard]]
match   = "shell(command=git push)"
when    = ["+shell(command=git status)"]
message = "Review changes before pushing."

Layer
When it runs
What it does

Guards
Before a tool call
Deny by capability, argument regex, and session history. A match returns a denial instead of executing the call.

Hooks
After a tool result
A non-zero exit injects stdout into the agent's inbox — lint and format failures become automatic corrections without restarting the turn.

Validators
After a turn
Scripts the agent reads on its next turn. This replaces "approve this change?" prompts in autonomous loops.

If you know Claude Code hooks: guards are PreToolUse denies declared in TOML, hooks are PostToolUse, validators are Stop — no scripts required for the common cases.
Hook and validator script examples: Guardrails guide.

The same harness, exposed wherever your workflow needs it.

Need machine-readable results? Pass --schema schema.json to constrain the final response to a JSON Schema (requires a model with structured-output support). See Structured output.

Agent Plugins (plugin.json + skills + mcp.json) from taps, .agents/plugins/, or ~/.config/agents/plugins/; project AGENTS.md loads at session start

A second model plans, checks completion, and condenses tool output; lessons persist as files per project and role

--sandbox locks writes to the working directory via Landlock (Linux) or Seatbelt (macOS), inherited by every shell, MCP server, and sub-agent

Token efficiency
Cache-aware cost accounting and adaptive compression

octomind run developer:general    # general dev, language skills auto-activate
octomind run doctor:blood         # blood-test interpretation specialist
octomind run lawyer:sg            # legal specialist
Running a specialist fetches its manifest from the tap registry, installs any required binaries, resolves credentials, starts the right MCP servers, and then opens the session.
Build and register your own:
octomind tap init yourteam/my-tap   # scaffold, validate, git-init, and register locally
octomind tap yourteam/my-tap        # on another machine, after publishing to GitHub
The octomind- prefix is added automatically: yourteam/my-tap maps to the repository
yourteam/octomind-my-tap.

articles.sourceTitle: AI is forcing us to pay off 40 years of technical debt
articles.title: PHP2Shell Is a Wakeup Call for AI in Cybersecurity
articles.text: In late October, a slew of major cybersecurity issues came to light. But none were bigger than the so-called PHP2Shell vulnerability, which put a plethora of websites, including those of NASA, Wikipedia, the White House, and all other sites that run on Wordpress or Drupal (among others) at risk of exploits capable of both reading sensitive data and running malicious code on the host server.As far as anyone is aware, disaster has been averted: The hack was discovered by cybersecurity researchers who reported it to the PHP Foundation, and a patch was released before any bad actors got their hands on the exploit. However, PHP2Shell may be the canary in the coal mine, serving as a warning sign for what’s to come in the age of AI.“One of the things we’re witnessing now is that all the legacy software that was written by humans over the last 40 years is being exposed,” says Matt Suiche, AI security research lead at the cybersecurity startup Tolmo. “Now it is time for the technical debt to be paid off.”PHP Legacy Bug and Memory ErrorsPHP, which originally stood for “personal home page,” is a programming language created back in 1994 and largely used by legacy sites. The bug underlying the PHP2Shell vulnerability was reported to the PHP Foundation as far back as 2024. The bug caused a common type of issue called an out-of-memory error, in which the amount of memory allocated to a piece of data is too small to hold the data. Normally, this type of error causes the program to crash—an unpleasant but not inherently dangerous result. And so the bug remained unaddressed.“If you look at any at any point of time, there will be a bunch of bug reports that are waiting to be fixed, which are just crashes. Most people don’t take them very seriously,” says Suman Jana, an associate professor of computer science at Columbia University.“It’s just that it’s a lot of very specific reasoning that is painful to do. And AI, I think, has done a very good job at that.” –Suman Jana, Columbia UniversityEarlier this year, the cybersecurity firm Calif offered to independently audit PHP, sponsored by OpenAI. Within two weeks, a researcher at Calif, aided by AI tools, found a way to use the out-of-memory bug to run arbitrary code on the host server, allowing a malicious actor to install malware or read critical data. Now, it was no longer a minor bug—it was a critical vulnerability, and the Calif team alerted the PHP foundation to start working on a patch immediately.Jana says actually exploiting the bug requires carefully working out a way to jump to a specific point in the memory for a particular program running on the server, and work out exactly which bits to overwrite in what order to gain control of the system. “It’s not really rocket science,” he says. “It’s just that it’s a lot of very specific reasoning that is painful to do. And AI, I think, has done a very good job at that.”To be clear, the researchers at Calif (as well as OpenAI and Wiz, a cybersecurity company that confirmed and expanded the vulnerabilities) had deep knowledge of both cybersecurity and the PHP language. “I’m not claiming that AI can do it all by itself. It clearly cannot,” Jana says. “But it is improving a lot, so the top 0.1 percent [of experts] can get a lot more stuff done, and also just below the 0.1 percent now will be able to go there without understanding all the nitty-gritty details.”AI Tools and Formal Verification in SecurityAfter the exploits were disclosed to the PHP Foundation, a team of four engineers spent two months developing a patch to release as quickly as possible.“There is a fundamental asymmetry in finding bugs and fixing bugs,” Jana says. “Because when you’re fixing bugs you have to make sure that you know all parts of that attack are closed, and also that you don’t break any existing functionality.”This asymmetry puts a lot of strain on the defenders, especially for open-source software such as PHP. Maintaining open-source projects that don’t have clear revenue streams despite being widely used is a long-standing challenge that precedes AI hacking tools. But those tools make the issue more pressing than ever. One way to stay ahead of such issues going forward is to empower the defenders with more money and access to frontier cybersecurity AI models. “These frontier labs are donating some of their token budgets to look into these bugs, which I think is great,” Jana says. “I think that should happen more, either through some concerted effort or through donations.”Jana is also optimistic that formal verification tools to automate the patching side of the equation are also advancing quickly, including a new release from Anthropic on 22 October. “The patch is LLM-generated, and then an LLM generates the proof that the patch is correct,” says Jana. “The only thing not done by an LLM is the proof checker, because somebody has to check the proof, because LLMs hallucinate. So, you want something that is formal.”Hopefully, the combination of specialized AI models and formal verification tools will make patching vulnerabilities nearly as automatable as finding them. Matthew Green, an associate professor of computer science at Johns Hopkins University Information Security Institute, is less optimistic. “Nobody’s going to fix this problem until something really bad happens,” he says. “And PHP2Shell wasn’t bad enough to be really bad. So when something really bad happens, which is going to be maybe sometime in early 2027, something bad that normal people are upset by, then suddenly people will start doing this. We’re going to fund everything.”In the meantime, Green says, update your software. “If your phone is like, ‘Hey, there’s a security update available, do you want to install it,’ don’t wait till next week. Just do it.”One thing’s for sure—PHP2Shell is just the beginning. “This won’t be the last one for sure,” Jana says. “It’s just who finds it. Hopefully, the white-hat hackers find it first, like this one.”

articles.sourceTitle: Nvidia RTX Spark encrypted firmware slows inference speed to 35% on Linux
articles.title: Linux on the Nvidia RTX Spark Laptop: What Actually Works
articles.text:
Can you run Linux on the Nvidia RTX Spark laptop?
Yes, but it comes with a serious catch. Linux installs and runs on RTX Spark laptops like the MSI Prestige N16 Flip AI Plus, including GPU acceleration through Nvidia’s open kernel driver. The problem is clock speed: once the laptop is plugged into wall power, the GPU gets locked to roughly 780 MHz on Linux instead of the 2 GHz-plus it hits on Windows. That turns a chip capable of around 65 tokens per second on a 120 billion parameter model into one struggling to break 14 tokens per second, for reasons tied to power management firmware that Linux currently can’t read.
TL;DR

Dual-booting Linux works on the MSI Prestige RTX Spark laptop, with a full desktop, GPU acceleration via Nvidia’s open driver, 4K output at 120Hz, and working audio, keyboard, and touchpad once configured correctly.
A hidden Windows-only component called the Nvidia Platform Controllers and Framework manages power delivery between CPU and GPU, and it has no Linux equivalent, which is the root cause of the slowdown.
GPU clock speed collapses to about 780 MHz on Linux when plugged in, compared to roughly 2.2 GHz on Windows, because the firmware’s power table is encrypted and only the Windows driver can decrypt it.
Benchmarks on GPT-OSS-120B show the gap clearly: Windows hit 65.4 tokens per second, WSL hit 65.1, the Nvidia DGX Spark hit 61, and native Linux on the same laptop managed only 13.9.
Memory allocation is a separate headache, since the laptop reserves 96GB of unified memory for the GPU by default and only Windows exposes a setting to change that split, which is required before Linux can see more than a sliver of RAM.
WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) is the practical middle ground today, since it rides on the Windows driver stack and keeps full GPU boost whether the laptop is plugged in or on battery, while still running Linux-first AI tools like vLLM.
A real fix depends on Nvidia, specifically on porting the platform controller’s power management logic into its Linux driver, which would effectively turn the laptop into a portable version of the DGX Spark.

Self-host
Remy.On-prem or in your private cloud. Remy and every app you build stay inside your walls.
What makes the RTX Spark laptop different from a normal Windows PC?
The RTX Spark platform, which ships in machines like the MSI Prestige, the Asus ProArt, and the Dell XPS, uses the same GPU design as Nvidia’s DGX Spark desktop unit. But where the DGX Spark ships with Nvidia’s own Linux build out of the box, every one of these laptop variants ships with Windows on ARM.
That distinction matters because Windows on ARM with CUDA support is new. ARM-based Windows machines have existed for a few years, but pairing that architecture with Nvidia’s CUDA stack only became possible with this chip. The laptops also support unified memory configurations up to 128GB, shared between CPU and GPU, which is unusual for a laptop and central to why they’re being marketed at AI developers in the first place.
Because so much of the AI tooling ecosystem, including vLLM and SGLang, is built Linux-first, developers who buy these machines naturally want to know whether they can ditch Windows, or at least dual-boot, without losing performance.
How do you actually install Linux on it?
The process is not plug-and-play. A first attempt using Omarchy (a Linux distribution with Arch roots) failed because, while it already supported the chip on Asus and Dell hardware, the MSI Prestige behaved differently, producing a flickering, unstable display during boot.
Switching to Debian worked more reliably, but still needed workarounds. The installer couldn’t connect to Wi-Fi, so installation required a USB Ethernet adapter. Out of the box, Debian also didn’t recognize the keyboard, touchpad, or GPU, because none of the laptop-specific hardware support was present in a vanilla kernel.
Going back to Omarchy solved the driver problem, since its kernel already bundled Nvidia’s open-source driver. At that point Linux booted properly, but could only see 28GB of the laptop’s 128GB of unified memory. That’s because the laptop’s firmware reserves 96GB for GPU use, and that split is only adjustable from Windows. Dropping the Windows-side GPU memory reservation down to 4GB freed up 120GB for Linux to see once booted. After that adjustment, the laptop ran a full desktop at 4K and 120Hz, with working audio, touchpad, keyboard, and CUDA acceleration.
Getting video output over HDMI during the install process was its own obstacle. Early in the process, the laptop would only display video on its own internal screen, not over HDMI, which required pointing an external camera at the laptop’s screen just to see what was happening during remote-controlled installation steps.
How does Linux performance compare to Windows and WSL?
This is where the story turns. With GPT-OSS-120B running on the GPU, Windows produced 65.4 tokens per second. WSL, which runs a Linux environment inside Windows, hit 65.1 tokens per second, nearly identical. The DGX Spark desktop unit, running Nvidia’s native Linux build, came in at 61 tokens per second. Native Linux on the laptop, however, dropped to 13.9 tokens per second, roughly five times slower.

The gap showed up again with vLLM running eight concurrent clients: WSL reached 127 tokens per second while native Linux reached 39.5. A longer benchmark run told the same story in time rather than throughput. Windows finished in about 8 minutes while holding the GPU near 2.2 GHz. Linux took 37 minutes, with the GPU parked around 790 MHz the entire time. Temperatures stayed low, between 40 and 47°C, so this isn’t a thermal throttling issue. The GPU simply isn’t being allowed to run at full speed.
Oddly, the direction of the problem flips depending on power source. Unplugged, Linux hit around 61 to 67 tokens per second on LM Studio, comparable to Windows. Plugged in, that same test dropped to about 15 tokens per second. Clock speed told the same story: around 1,800 MHz unplugged under load, and down to roughly 780 MHz when connected to wall power.
Why does plugging in the laptop slow Linux down?
The cause traces back to a component visible in Windows Device Manager called the Nvidia Platform Controllers and Framework. This piece of firmware and driver logic manages the shared power budget between CPU and GPU, since a laptop (unlike the desktop DGX Spark) has to balance power delivery between both chips rather than feeding the GPU on its own line.
Disabling that controller in Windows reproduced the slowdown directly: tokens per second dropped from around 83 to about 31, and clock speed fell from roughly 2 GHz down to the same 786 MHz seen on Linux when plugged in. Re-enabling the controller restored normal speed immediately. That confirms the controller, not the kernel, the distribution, or the Nvidia GPU driver itself, is what’s holding Linux back.
The deeper issue is that the firmware hands this controller a table of power settings that is encrypted. Windows has the key to decrypt it. Linux currently does not, and no software fix attempted during testing could enable it, including one attempt that triggered a kernel panic. Extracting the decryption key from the Windows driver was floated as a theoretical workaround, but that would amount to a fragile, single-machine hack rather than something that works broadly. A real fix needs to come from Nvidia shipping equivalent power management logic in its Linux driver.
Is WSL a good substitute for native Linux right now?
For most developers, yes, at least for now. WSL runs on top of the Windows driver stack, so it inherits Windows’ full GPU boost behavior whether the laptop is plugged in or running on battery. It also runs Linux-first AI tools like vLLM and SGLang without the clock throttling problem that affects native Linux installs.
The one adjustment needed is memory. WSL reserves only 14GB by default, which isn’t enough for large model workloads on a 128GB unified memory machine, so that allocation needs to be increased manually. Once that’s done, WSL benchmarks land close to native Windows performance, making it the more practical choice until Nvidia addresses the Linux driver gap directly.

Does unplugging the laptop fix the Linux performance problem?
It helps significantly. On battery power, Linux GPU clocks and token throughput come much closer to Windows levels. The severe slowdown specifically appears when the laptop is plugged into wall power, which is the opposite of what most users would expect.
Is WSL the same as running native Linux on the RTX Spark?
Not exactly, but it’s close in practice. WSL runs a Linux environment on top of the Windows kernel and driver stack, so it retains Windows’ GPU clock boost behavior and avoids the throttling issue, while still supporting Linux-native AI tools like vLLM.
Will Nvidia fix Linux GPU performance on RTX Spark laptops?
That depends on Nvidia shipping the platform controller’s power management logic in its Linux driver. The encrypted firmware power table currently can only be decrypted by Windows, and no workaround found so far restores full clock speed on Linux without it.
